lines.text: Do you know the Eiffel Tower is taller in summer?
This is the Eiffel Tower. Seven thousand three hundred tonnes of iron, standing over three hundred metres above Paris.
It's built from puddled iron, an early kind of wrought iron. And like every metal, it grows when it gets warm.
Iron stretches about twelve millionths of its length for every degree. Over three hundred metres, a hot summer day can make the tower about fifteen centimetres taller.
On a freezing winter night, it shrinks back down.
But the sun never heats it evenly. It shines on one side, and that side grows more than the side in the shade.
So the top bends away from the sun. By up to eighteen centimetres.
And as the sun crosses the sky, the top follows it, drawing a slow curve through the air. Every single day.
To build it, Gustave Eiffel's team made eighteen thousand and thirty-eight iron parts.
And joined them with two and a half million rivets.
Each rivet was heated until it glowed red, pushed through the holes, and hammered flat.
As it cooled, it shrank, and pulled the plates together tighter than a bolt ever could.
And all that open lattice lets the wind pass straight through. In a storm, the top sways only about nine centimetres.
Eiffel said his biggest worry was the wind. So the curve of the four legs comes straight from his wind calculations.
It adapts to the conditions. So does Orbi Transfer.
It tries the direct path between your two devices first.
And when it can't, it uses an encrypted copy in the cloud. Locked before it ever leaves your device.
